assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks, built on Katori's magic-wavelength proposal, push fractional uncertainty to the 1e-18 level and redefine what can be measured. This is the clearest case of a measurement technique opening new science (relativistic geodesy, tests of fundamental constants, dark-matter searches) and underpins the coming redefinition of the second. Experimental demonstration with measured systematics is exactly what I value.
assessment.attribution: The credited list is a clean two-person configuration: Katori for the magic-wavelength lattice concept and first Sr clock, Ye for the record accuracy and stability and the comb-linked clock network. Other groups (e.g. Lemonde, Ludlow, Lisdat, Sterr) contributed but the pair is defensible.
assessment.maturity: Multiple independent labs have reproduced and surpassed each other's results over about two decades, and the interpretation is stable. Timing is good, though the SI redefinition has not yet happened.
uncertainties: Hall and Hänsch already received the 2005 prize for the comb, so the novelty must be judged on the lattice clock itself.
Some members may see ion clocks (Wineland, Rosenband) as overlapping prior recognition.
Whether the redefinition of the second should come first is a timing question I cannot settle.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Atom interferometry turned matter-wave coherence into a precision sensor for gravity, rotation and the fine-structure constant, and is now used in tests of equivalence principle and gravity-gradient measurements. It fits my view that physics is limited by how precisely we can measure.
assessment.attribution: Bordé (Ramsey-Bordé interferometer theory and early realisation), Pritchard (first atom interferometers with material gratings) and Kasevich (light-pulse interferometers with precision gravimetry) form a natural trio. Chu and others are not credited on the longlist; I cannot judge their role from this list alone.
assessment.maturity: Well confirmed across many groups, with commercial gravimeters and gradiometers in use. Competing early demonstrations (Mlynek, Carnal; Chu and Kasevich) complicate credit but the field is mature.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 1997 and 2001 prizes for laser cooling and condensates, and unclear priority among early demonstrations.
Real-world sensitivity advantages over classical instruments are still being demonstrated.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit QED provided the architecture for strong coupling of superconducting qubits to resonators, enabling dispersive readout, gates and error-correction experiments. It is the working base of current superconducting quantum processors and has opened a whole field with real device impact.
assessment.attribution: Blais proposed the architecture with Huang, Wallraff and Girvin; Schoelkopf and Wallraff made the first strong-coupling demonstration. The proposed trio is reasonable, though Girvin and Devoret share credit and the 2025 prize on macroscopic tunnelling touched adjacent work.
assessment.maturity: Extensively reproduced by many groups and industrial teams; maturity is high but the technology is still evolving.
uncertainties: Close proximity to the most recent superconducting-circuit prize could be seen as either supportive or redundant.
Credit split between theory and experiment and omitted names such as Girvin.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical readout and coherent control of single defect spins, especially NV centres, enabled nanoscale magnetometry, thermometry and biological sensing at ambient conditions. It is a new measurement modality with growing impact beyond physics, similar in spirit to my own medical-imaging turn.
assessment.attribution: Wrachtrup demonstrated single NV optical detection of magnetic resonance, Awschalom pioneered coherent control and spin qubits in defects, Lukin led sensing and quantum register work. A fair three-person configuration, though Walsworth and others also contributed.
assessment.maturity: Very widely reproduced and extended; sensing applications are beginning to be used in practice, although many remain at the demonstration stage.
uncertainties: The compound nature (single-spin detection, quantum control, sensing) may need an agreed focus.
Lukin also appears on other candidates, which affects portfolio balance.
Practical sensitivity advantages in biology are still being established.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Rydberg blockade yields strongly interacting, individually addressable atoms in tweezer arrays, giving programmable quantum simulators and a leading quantum-computing platform. Experiments show high-fidelity gates and large-scale many-body simulation.
assessment.attribution: Zoller and Lukin proposed the blockade-based gates, Browaeys demonstrated blockade of single atoms and array experiments, and Saffman worked on gate protocols. The credit is spread across several groups, so a three-person selection is somewhat arbitrary.
assessment.maturity: Rapidly developing and independently confirmed, but the long-term outcome of the platform is not yet settled, so recognition may be a little early.
uncertainties: Attribution among theory proposals and the first blockade experiments (Browaeys, Grangier, Gould, Saffman) is contested.
Premature if neutral-atom quantum computing has not yet shown clear advantage.
Overlap with candidates crediting Zoller or Lukin.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The qPlus sensor and CO-functionalised tips gave atomic-resolution AFM, imaging of bond order and molecular structure in real space. It is a genuine instrumentation advance that changed what can be observed on surfaces and in on-surface chemistry.
assessment.attribution: Giessibl invented the qPlus sensor, Meyer and Gross (IBM Zurich) demonstrated the functionalised-tip imaging of molecules. Binnig, Quate and Gerber were earlier AFM inventors, and the 1986 prize recognised STM, so the credited trio is clear for this refinement.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced in many labs and commercially adopted; interpretation is stable. The question is whether this is a refinement of AFM rather than a new discovery of the scale expected.
uncertainties: Incremental nature relative to the earlier AFM invention.
Whether the committee considers this physics versus chemistry.
Lasting broad scientific impact beyond surface science is limited so far.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical coherence tomography is a transformative measurement technique, now standard in ophthalmology and used in cardiology, with real impact beyond physics. As someone working on optical tissue imaging I know how difficult it is to take such a method from idea to routine clinical use.
assessment.attribution: Huang, Swanson and Fujimoto (with Fercher's earlier work and Izatt, Tearney and others) shaped the initial demonstration and development. The credited group is reasonable, but priority questions with Fercher and Hitzenberger, and with low-coherence reflectometry, are unresolved.
assessment.maturity: Fully mature, with decades of clinical deployment; timing is not a concern.
uncertainties: Strong applied and medical character may be judged outside the physics prize remit.
Credit disputes with earlier low-coherence interferometry work and the wider developer community.
The fundamental physics novelty is limited.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene created a tunable platform for correlated insulators and unconventional superconductivity, and launched moiré materials research with many follow-up discoveries. Experimentally it opened a field with tunable parameters accessible by simple gating.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald predicted the flat band at the magic angle; Jarillo-Herrero's group demonstrated correlated insulators and superconductivity. Andrei contributed independently to the experimental and earlier theoretical understanding, which complicates a three-person split.
assessment.maturity: Quickly and widely reproduced, but the superconducting mechanism remains unsettled and sample variability is a known problem, so the mature picture is still forming.
uncertainties: Mechanism of superconductivity is still debated.
Reproducibility depends on twist-angle disorder.
Credit between Andrei, Jarillo-Herrero and the theorists is unresolved.
